This isn’t just anime… it’s a memory drawn in pain.

Hadashi no Gen (Barefoot Gen, 1983) is a Japanese animated film directed by Mori Masaki that depicts the Atomic bombing of Hiroshima and its immediate aftermath from the perspective of civilians—particularly that of a child. Although its animation style initially appears simple, it starkly contrasts with the film’s explicit depictions of destruction, burned bodies, and widespread chaos. By avoiding spectacle or heroic framing, the film rejects any sense of glorification and stands as one of the most uncompromising anti-war portrayals in animated cinema. Its raw realism led to its use as educational material in Japan, while also making it controversial, resulting in censorship or restricted circulation in certain contexts.

The film is based on the manga of the same name created by Keiji Nakazawa, published between 1973 and 1985. The manga is a deeply autobiographical work inspired by Nakazawa’s own experience as a survivor of the Hiroshima bombing. It follows the life of Gen Nakaoka before and after the attack, portraying not only the explosion and immediate devastation but also the long-term consequences—hunger, poverty, trauma, radiation sickness, and the discrimination faced by survivors in the postwar years. With its direct narrative style and refusal to soften the realities it depicts, Hadashi no Gen became a significant part of Japanese historical memory and one of the most powerful critiques of militarism and war in modern manga.
